GRU airport does not have subway or train service to São Paulo. Taxis from GRU expensive (about R$120-150). This leaves us with bus service.

There are two types of bus service to and from GRU.

The usual choice is called "Airport Bus Service." It costs R$42.00, has nice coach style buses, and takes you to the main locations and hotels. That's what most tourists take and it’s overpriced, in my opinion.

Option B is the lesser known 257 line and it is a regular city bus taken by the ordinary folk. It is operated by EMTU, costs R$5.15, has fairly decent city buses and takes you to the closest subway station. Definitely the best cost-benefit option. At the airport information counter, say or show a note saying "ônibus EMTU linha 257 para Metrô Tatuapé". You pay the fare on board, to the collector ("cobrador"). Once you arrive at the Tatuapé station, you can take the subway to the main São Paulo districts for R$3.50. Source: EMTU website.
How to go from GRU airport to São Paulo for less than R$10.

Distros like Mint can set up the Dualboot for you automatically, however, you first need to shrink the space that your Windows 10 installation is on. According to my research (I haven't used Windows 10, but I have done this exact thing on Windows 7), you can do this by right clicking on "My Computer", selecting manage, and then selecting Disk Management. Just locate the largest chunk of space (called a partition) and shrink that by half.

Make sure you back up your data and have an install media for Windows 10 ready, though. It doesn't always happen, but resizing these chunks of space on your drive can mess with the integrity of the data.

After that, just fire up your install media of Linux Mint, fire up the installer, and when it asks you where you want to install, select "Install Alongside Other Operating Systems" (I'm paraphrasing, here: it's been quite a while since I've done a Mint install, but it should say something like that). The Installer will detect that you've got Windows 10 installed, set up the space that Mint will live in, and then set up the bootloader that will allow you to choose between Mint and Windows when you fire up your computer.

Happy Linuxing!

Well, in one case it is for everyone and in one case it is just for you, but you only experience the world from yourself, so for you the effects are identical. I am not bending words around here. It is you who is saying that because two things have different words that their effect on you must be different. They are not. They are literally the same from your perspective. I would also like to point out the humor in your selectively leaving out sentences of mine that undermine your argument. "This is irrelevant because we are talking about blocking (user's choice) not banning (admin's choice)". Please read again the line where I said blocking is when "you are your own admin". Taking this into consideration your quote reads "This is irrelevant because we are talking about blocking (admin's choice) not banning (admin's choice)". Anyway since you seem to have some sort of power complex about the difference between admin's and users, I don't have to use those words. My argument stands regardless of whether or not you can see that blocking subverses is you policing yourself.

Again, don't get me wrong on this. You absolutely 100% without any exception should have the ability to block any subverse that you want. The question is about whether you should be able to block WITHOUT EVEN LOOKING AT THE CONTENT. When you block a subverse, you silence the voices of all those who speak on that subverse. No, not for everyone, but for yourself. You prevent yourself from hearing what other people have to say. Now to my point: we should seriously consider the impact of encouraging people to silence other people's views WITHOUT EVER HEARING THEM.

What are the disadvantages of NOT adding the one click button? You have to make 1, maybe 2, extra clicks to permanently silence a community that you do not wish to hear from, and of course you have to see the content you are blocking in between those clicks. How many subverses are you likely to block in total? 100? 1000? How many per day? 30 on the first day, 10 on the second, maybe 5 or 6 per day from then on? So you save maybe 10 clicks on average and have to see 20 seconds of content that you didn't want to see per day during your first month, and even less from then on? Do you see how that is a minuscule thing to complain about while you surf for hours and hours online? Are you such a fragile little flower that you can't handle less than 20 seconds per day of content that you don't like before you block it forever?

Now what are the disadvantages of adding the one click button? You might block something based off it's name because you assumed something about their culture and you were wrong. It is highly likely that you will never unblock the subverse and realize what you've missed. You will never know what you missed.

Maybe you are okay with that kind of self-deprivation as long as you never find out what you missed, but for the community it brews monoculture. Maybe a better analogy is "strains non-obvious culture" but that doesn't sound as catchy.

As a final note: my whole argument is that you should CONSIDER not having the button. I'm not even saying that not having the button is the best option. I'm saying that you shouldn't dismiss it without even thinking about the long term effects.
